passage:
Tuesday. On the phone, Afreen said, "I never told you not to come for Eid. You are imagining things. You are too sensitive." Zubin had the text on the screen: "Don't bother coming this year." For a moment the words on the screen felt less real than the voice. Zubin's stomach went cold.

Thursday. Zubin started a note on the phone: the date, what was said, what was written. Two lines. Writing it down felt like putting a foot on solid floor.

The following Sunday. Zubin told a cousin, who said, "Your mother did that to me over the wedding dates." Zubin sat still. The notes were enough, and Afreen did not have to say "you're right" for Zubin to trust them.

qa.q: What did the text on Zubin's screen say?
qa.a: It said, "Don't bother coming this year."

qa.q: Why did the words on the screen feel less real than the voice for a moment?
qa.a: Afreen's firm denial made Zubin doubt Zubin's own memory for a moment.

qa.q: How does the note help Zubin?
qa.a: A dated record of what was said and written gives Zubin something solid to trust, without needing Afreen's agreement.

qa.q: How does the cousin see Afreen's behaviour?
qa.a: The cousin says the mother did the same thing about the wedding dates, so the cousin sees a pattern rather than Zubin being too sensitive.

grounding: A parent denies what was said and calls the child too sensitive; the protagonist keeps notes, trusts direct experience and talks to a trusted person.

passage: Gargi, you look tired after the trip to your parents' house, so let me tell you about mine. At twenty-five, every visit home left me sour for days. My father had always compared me with my elder cousin and beaten me down with words whenever my marks slipped. The moment I walked into the flat, I turned twelve again and snapped at everything. One night, on the balcony, I said aloud, "It was unfair, and it still hurts." That was the first time I stopped arguing with the memory. I decided to visit for two days, not five, to leave the old topics alone, and I saw a counsellor. I never announced that my father was forgiven, and I never made him pay. I just stopped acting as if nothing had happened. Harsha

qa.q: How long did Harsha decide each visit should last?
qa.a: Harsha decided on two days instead of five.

qa.q: Why did saying it aloud on the balcony matter to Harsha?
qa.a: Harsha felt relief at admitting the hurt was real, and so stopped arguing with the memory.

qa.q: What steps did Harsha take to manage the visits home?
qa.a: Shorter visits, leaving the old topics alone, and seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: What would change if Harsha had chosen to punish the father forever?
qa.a: The resentment would stay in charge of Harsha's life instead of being acknowledged and managed.

grounding: An elder recalls carrying pain from an unfair childhood that flared on visits home, acknowledging it, choosing limits and seeing a counsellor.

passage:
"They said the power cut was my fault. I wasn't even home," said Yash.

"The meter is in the hall, and you were at the library," Aadhya said.

"I know. I apologised anyway. I always do."

"When did you last apologise for something that really was yours?"

Yash was quiet. "I can't remember. Something goes wrong and everyone's eyes come to me. Even my own eyes, now."

"That's your family's habit, not a fact about you."

"It feels like a fact."

"Try saying, 'This isn't mine.' Just once, at dinner."

"And then Baba goes silent for two days."

"Maybe. But you'd know that's him going quiet, not proof."

"Can I come to your study group on Sundays? I'd like somewhere else to be."

"Obviously. Bring your tea flask."

qa.q: Where was Yash when the power cut happened?
qa.a: Yash was at the library.

qa.q: What does Yash mean by "Even my own eyes, now"?
qa.a: Yash has begun to believe the family's blame and see Yash as the cause too, feeling guilty by habit even when not at fault.

qa.q: How could Yash build support and distance from the blame?
qa.a: By joining Aadhya's Sunday study group and calmly saying "This isn't mine" when blamed unfairly.

qa.q: How might Baba react to Yash speaking up?
qa.a: Yash expects Baba to go silent for two days, which shows the family's habit of pulling back when the role is challenged.

grounding: A family blames a member for everything; the protagonist starts to see it as a family pattern, not proof of worth, and seeks outside support.

passage: At Sunday lunch in São Paulo, Aunt Rosa passed the rice and asked, "And what do you earn now? Marta's daughter is already a manager." Then, "Still no ring, Beatriz?" Beatriz felt her cheeks heat and her fork go still. She smiled. "I earn enough to visit you, Tia, and the ring can wait for the right person." A cousin laughed. Aunt Rosa waved the serving spoon as if the subject were a fly. Later, while they washed dishes, Lindiwe bumped Beatriz's shoulder and said, "You handled that." Beatriz let out a long breath. "Every time she asks, I hear her worrying about her own daughters, not about me." Then she handed over the next plate.

qa.q: What did Beatriz reply about the ring?
qa.a: She said the ring could wait for the right person.

qa.q: What does Beatriz mean when she says she hears Aunt Rosa worrying about her own daughters?
qa.a: Beatriz feels the questions come from Aunt Rosa's own anxieties, not from Beatriz's worth.

qa.q: Which part of Beatriz's reply kept the peace, and why?
qa.a: Her light, brief tone with a smile ended the topic without a fight.

qa.q: How might Aunt Rosa have experienced the reply?
qa.a: Aunt Rosa waved the serving spoon as if the subject were a fly, which suggests she took it as small talk and was not offended.

grounding: Relatives compare the protagonist's salary and marriage status; she answers briefly and lightly and sees the questions as their anxieties.

passage: Nikita had come home to the village for Ganesh Chaturthi after eight months in Pune. At the courtyard well, her mother Tanuja did not look up. "You left us for a salary," she said to the bucket. The neighbours' ears seemed to grow. Nikita's face burned; she wanted to shout that she sent money and called every night. Instead she took the other handle of the bucket and said, "I missed the smell of this courtyard, Aai. I am not coming back to live here, but I will be here every festival, and I will call on Sundays." Tanuja's lips tightened, yet she let Nikita carry the water. That night Tanuja set aside the first modak for her.

qa.q: How long had Nikita been in Pune before the visit?
qa.a: Nikita had been in Pune for eight months.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel and want to do when her mother spoke to the bucket?
qa.a: Her face burned, and she wanted to shout that she sent money and called every night, but she held back.

qa.q: How did Nikita show love while staying firm on her decision?
qa.a: She helped carry the water, promised to be there every festival and call on Sundays, and said she was not coming back to live there.

qa.q: What might Tanuja's setting aside the first modak for Nikita suggest?
qa.a: Tanuja is softening and shows love in her own way, even though her words were sharp.

grounding: A family says the protagonist abandoned them for work; she feels guilt and anger, shows love in ways she can and stays firm on her choice.

passage: Minakshi found a yellowed school report in the steel trunk at her mother's flat in Kolkata. Bhavna had been first in class at eleven, and a pencil note said, "Withdrawn, family needs." Minakshi read it standing in the hallway and thought of the years of sharp words about wasted rupees and the marks-or-nothing rule. Something in her softened, and sadness came with it. "Ma, you never went back to school, did you?" "No time," Bhavna said, taking the paper gently. Minakshi sat beside her and said nothing for a while. She did not say the past was fine. But that evening, when Bhavna began to raise her voice about the wedding budget, Minakshi said kindly, "Ma, I will talk when we can both be calm," and ended the call softly.

qa.q: What did the pencil note on the school report say?
qa.a: The note said, "Withdrawn, family needs."

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling in the hallway?
qa.a: Something softened in her, with sadness, as she began to see where her mother's harshness might have come from.

qa.q: How did Minakshi keep a boundary while feeling compassion?
qa.a: She said she would talk when both could be calm and ended the call softly.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt when Minakshi read the report?
qa.a: Bhavna took the paper gently and said there had been no time, which suggests an old loss she does not dwell on.

grounding: The protagonist sees a parent's harshness came from pain and poverty, feels sadness and softness, and still holds a boundary.

passage:
Friday. At dinner Sunaina's father Vikas announced that a match was "more or less fixed" and that the wedding would follow once her posting in Bhopal ended. Sunaina's rice went cold. "I would like to talk about this, Papa," she said. "What is there to discuss?" he replied.

Sunday. On the terrace she told her mother and her aunt that she was not refusing marriage; she wanted a say in whom and when. Her aunt said, "I will speak to your father."

Next Saturday. Sunaina asked her father to hear her for ten minutes without interrupting: two years to finish her fellowship, then she would gladly meet families. Vikas was silent a while. "Two years? Let me talk to your mother." She had no yes, but she had a maybe, and she had not shouted.

qa.q: What did Sunaina ask her father for on Saturday?
qa.a: She asked him to hear her for ten minutes without interrupting.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when her rice went cold?
qa.a: Sunaina was shocked and pinned between love for her family and her own wishes.

qa.q: How did Sunaina gather support?
qa.a: She talked to her mother and her aunt on the terrace, and her aunt offered to speak to her father.

qa.q: How might Vikas be seeing the situation?
qa.a: Vikas assumed the match was settled and saw little to discuss, but his "let me talk to your mother" shows he is starting to listen.

grounding: A family expects the protagonist to follow their marriage plan; she explains calmly, gathers allies and chooses how firmly to hold her ground.

passage:
Dear Joseph,

You asked why I did not come to Diwali dinner, so I will tell you plainly. Three months ago I stopped answering my father's calls. There were years of shouting and cutting remarks, and after my brother's wedding it got worse. The first week I felt lighter and slept through the night. In the second week I cried in the supermarket over a packet of his favourite biscuits. I keep asking myself whether I am punishing him. I do not think so. I think I am protecting myself. Still, I have written a note to myself: if he ever changes, and when I know I am safe, I will listen. For now I am keeping the door on the latch.

Love,
Anjali

qa.q: How long ago did Anjali stop answering the father's calls?
qa.a: Anjali stopped answering three months ago.

qa.q: What does Anjali's crying in the supermarket suggest?
qa.a: The relief is mixed with grief, and Anjali still misses something about the father.

qa.q: How can Anjali check that this comes from clarity and not anger?
qa.a: By asking whether the aim is protecting oneself rather than punishing, as Anjali does, and keeping the door ajar only where safety allows.

qa.q: Why might Joseph have asked about the missed dinner?
qa.a: Joseph noticed Anjali's absence and probably cares and is puzzled or worried.

grounding: The writer has cut contact with a father after long pain, feels relief mixed with grief, checks the motive and leaves the door only latched.

passage:
Rajni: Meera hasn't answered in five months. not one reply
Vishal: I know. Have you thought about why?
Rajni: I keep going back to the day I told my daughter in front of everyone that marrying him was a mistake. And the times I read her diary. I never said sorry
Vishal: Will you write to her?
Rajni: One letter. Only an apology. I won't ask her to come home. And I won't call her friends or the aunts any more. I did last year and I think it pushed her further
Vishal: That sounds right. Will you explain yourself in it?
Rajni: No. She decides what happens next
Vishal: I'll sit with you when you write it
Rajni: Thank you. It hurts. But I'd rather she comes back slowly than never

qa.q: How long has Meera not replied?
qa.a: Meera has not replied for five months.

qa.q: What does Rajni feel about the public remark and the diary?
qa.a: Rajni feels regret and sees these as hurtful acts, for which Rajni never apologised.

qa.q: What is Rajni's plan for the letter?
qa.a: One letter with only an apology, without asking Meera to come home and without explaining or defending.

qa.q: How might Meera have felt about the earlier calls to her friends and the aunts?
qa.a: Pressured and pushed further away, as Rajni suspects.

grounding: A parent whose child has cut contact feels hurt, plans an apology without defending, stops pressuring through relatives, and lets the child decide.

passage: After the Sunday class at the community centre, Aparna stayed on the lobby bench with a blank card from the notice-board tray. Six years since she and her brother Akash last spoke. She wrote three openings and crossed out all of them. The instructor passed with a bunch of keys and asked whether she needed anything; Aparna said, "Just a difficult note." What she finally wrote was: "Akash, it has been too long. I said cruel things about your wedding and never took them back. I am sorry. You do not have to reply. I would like to hear how you are, whenever you want." She did not add a list of who had hurt whom. At the post box outside, her hand paused. Then the card went in.

qa.q: How many years since Aparna and Akash last spoke?
qa.a: It has been six years.

qa.q: What might Aparna's paused hand at the post box show?
qa.a: Nervousness about reaching out and fear of how Akash will respond, before she decides to go ahead.

qa.q: What in the note leaves Akash room to decide?
qa.a: It says Akash does not have to reply and asks for news only whenever Akash wants.

qa.q: How might Akash feel on receiving the card?
qa.a: He may feel surprised, wary or moved, and the lack of demands lets him respond at his own pace.

grounding: The protagonist reaches out to a sibling after years of silence with a short humble note that owns her part and demands no accounting.
